title: Credit Cards for Newcomers to Canada with No Credit History: Big Five Banks vs Secured Cards
desc: RBC, TD, Scotiabank, CIBC and BMO all run newcomer card programs that don't require Canadian credit history; if declined, secured cards like Neo are the fallback. Limits and conditions compared.
body:
Bottom line: you can get a credit card in Canada without local credit history. All Big Five banks (RBC, TD, Scotiabank, CIBC, BMO) run newcomer card programs whose official pages say Canadian credit history is not required; if you're declined, a secured card is the fallback.

Compiled from each bank's newcomer pages (checked November 2026). Different pages for the same program sometimes disagree—re-check the official site or call before you apply.

Big Five newcomer cards compared

Bank / programLimit (as advertised)Who can applyWatch out for
Scotiabank StartRightUnsecured, up to $15,000PRs within 5 years, international students, foreign workersJoin StartRight first; card applications need an income letter from a Canadian employer; foreign workers also need a work permit and Canadian government ID. Partners with Nova Credit to use home-country credit for a higher limit
RBC Newcomer AdvantageUp to $15,000, no credit history requiredNewcomers (pages differ: some say within 5 years, others PRs within 12 months and work-permit holders within 48 months)Must be an RBC personal banking client; higher limits depend on income; secured vs unsecured may depend on your status
TD New to CanadaUp to $15,000PRs or temporary residents in Canada 5 years or less (not tourists or visitors)Limit based on verifiable income and any credit history; not available if you already hold a TD credit card
CIBC newcomer cardsNo fixed figure; at CIBC's discretionCanadian residents (age thresholds differ between pages)Says no income, credit history or deposit needed; the higher-limit offer requires showing immigration documents (IMM5292/IMM5688) in branch
BMO newcomer cardsUnsecured, up to $5,000PRs or foreign workers arrived within 5 yearsShow PR card, confirmation of PR or work permit (IMM 1442); if not approved unsecured, a secured card with deposit is possible

How to choose: for higher limits, start with Scotiabank, RBC or TD (all advertise up to $15,000)—but “up to” isn't a promise; your actual limit depends mostly on verifiable income. If you have good credit history abroad, look at Scotiabank's Nova Credit partnership.

Declined? Secured cards

A secured card needs an upfront deposit that roughly equals your limit—made for people with no credit history. For example:

  • Neo Secured Mastercard: Ratehub and Neo say deposits can start around $50 with no credit check; NerdWallet's review of the Tim Hortons co-branded version lists a $500 minimum. Versions differ—check Neo's site.
  • BMO also says you can get a secured card if not approved for an unsecured one.

Deposits are generally returned only when you close the account or graduate to an unsecured card, so only deposit money you won't need soon.

FAQ

Can I apply without a SIN?

It varies. TD and CIBC list a SIN on their application pages; RBC says a SIN is optional for opening an account. Get your SIN first if you can.

Can international students apply?

Scotiabank StartRight explicitly covers international students; CIBC has separate student cards with lower limits. Check other banks' sites.

Should I apply to several banks at once?

Each application usually triggers a credit inquiry. When starting out, get one card, pay on time for 6+ months, then consider a second.

Note: compiled from bank websites and comparison sites; limits and conditions change, so the official site prevails. Not financial advice.
